zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The supplied native BnF scan remains the authority for text, typeface and physical placement.

lines.note: Quagon denotes excessive words or overstatement; suguitaru supplies the idea of going beyond the measure. The scan prints cotaba, retained as an anomalous vowel sequence rather than silently changed to cotoba.
Quagon wo yuu means to speak excessively. The Portuguese Fa begins falar on the next row, but no terminal hyphen is visible and none is supplied.
Lar completes falar, 'speak with excess and arrogance'. This finishes the illustrative phrase rather than introducing another sense.
Hi ni itte shinuru explains dying after entering fire. The Portuguese describes self-immolation in a historical religious context; vi begins viuo without a printed hyphen.

runs.text: uo no fogo, & queimarſe como cuſtumão a fa-

lines.note: Uo completes viuo, and the gloss continues 'burn oneself, as some customarily do'. The fa- at this line end, unlike vi above, has a visible hyphen.
Zer completes fazer, with some Buddhist monks as the stated practitioners. This is the dictionary's historical account and supplies no additional procedural detail.

Quai first means an invitation to a tea gathering. Chanoyu is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese gloss and is retained in its locally italic type; Meǒchô begins the next-day invitation example.

The Japanese promises an invitation tomorrow morning. Both o-marks in mǒsǒzu are carons. Focused inspection places the Portuguese tilde over the first a after h in Amenhãa; retain this occurrence rather than imposing the final-a carrier documented on other pages.
Uidarei completes the invitation to Chanoyu. Item then begins a second sense, a gathering; the damaged Ajuntamen ends without a securely printed hyphen.
To completes ajuntamento, a gathering or recreation involving many people. Uta no quai introduces a poetry meeting, and the scan supplies a period after quai.
Tsuzumi no quai is a drum-playing meeting, paired with the poetry gathering above. The Portuguese starts explaining the activities associated with both examples.

runs.text: exercitão em fazer verſos, & ajuntamento dos

lines.note: The first gathering practises composing verses. The second half begins the parallel description of the people who practise instrumental playing.

runs.text: que ſe exercitão em tanger o tabaquinho.

lines.note: The second gathering practises playing the small drum. Tabaquinho is one printed Portuguese word, not OCR taba quinho; the tsuzumi example supplies its instrument context.
Hai and hokori identify ash and dust. The final t remains a checked ending, pò retains its grave, and S. is an upright written-register label.
Megurashibumi is a circulating letter. The Portuguese begins a letter 'that goes around', with its informational or directive purpose specified below.

runs.text: como de nouas, ou de outra couſa que ſe manda

lines.note: The circulating letter may contain news or something ordered to be carried out. The clause remains open until executar on the next line.
Executar completes the phrase about instructions sent round to be carried out. The short row closes Quaibun and is not omitted from the body.
Futokoro no uchi means inside the bosom or breast of a garment. The Portuguese ſe- begins ſeyo across the physical line break.
Yo belongs wholly to italic ſeyo, not to a Japanese fragment. The example repeats Quaichǔ with its caron, correcting OCR Quaichi; it means putting or carrying something in one's bosom.

runs.text: ſa, & leuala no ſeyo, ou conſigo pera caſa.

lines.note: The gloss continues taking an object and carrying it in the bosom, or taking it home. The preceding cou has no printed terminal hyphen, so the physical division is retained without one.
Kuni wo meguru means travelling around countries or provinces. The Portuguese begins 'go around, or ...', with the alternative continued below.
The alternative is travelling through various realms. The initial r of reinos is visible; OCR teinos is not a Portuguese word to preserve here.

Idaqi, u gives principal forms of the verb for embracing or holding in the arms. The o-mark of Quaifô is only partly inked; the draft's circumflex is retained as a chosen but uncertain reading. NINJAL 203c08 gives Quaifǒ, which is useful lexical evidence but cannot determine this copy's damaged accent.
Meguru kaze is a circling or revolving wind. The Portuguese begins a wind blowing round, with ventã- continued below.
Do completes the verb, and em roda specifies circular movement. The scan supports em roda, not OCR emnoda; the written-register S. is upright.
Kokoroyoku kataru means conversing pleasantly or freely. Portuguese praticar here is conversation, and à ſua continues with vontade below.
Vontade completes 'at one's ease or pleasure'. This closes the conversation gloss rather than modifying the following encounter entry.
Megurivǒ denotes meeting or encountering someone, with the old contracted form left intact. The Portuguese al- begins alguem across the break.
The person encountered has come from afar. Quaigǒ suru supplies the corresponding verbal example, with the same caron as the headword.
The example means making this encounter. Item then introduces a further meaning of Quaigǒ, whose repeated form is physically divided Quai-/gǒ.

runs.text: Ajuntamento que ſe faz de muitos pe-

lines.note: The additional meaning is an assembly of many people. The printed pe- begins pera, explaining the purpose of the assembly on the next row.
The gathering is for discussing and consulting about a matter. The nasal abbreviation in algũa is retained rather than expanded.
Hai and chiri give ash and dust or small particles. The Portuguese argueiro is damaged near the right rule, but its surviving strokes and the following ciſco support the reading.
Cisco is the additional dust or speck equivalent. Quaigin ni naru means becoming ash and dust; the Portuguese reflexive phrase continues below.
The example ends 'turn into dust and ash'. Poo is retained as the historical spelling and is not reduced to modern pó.

Quaijen is an expression of pleasure used in letters. The letter immediately after y in Cocoroyocu has an open, c-like outline under enlargement; the aligned reading with a worn o is retained as a nonblocking choice. Xicanari and the following Portuguese explanation remain as printed.

runs.text: vſada nas cartas, com que hum agradece, ou

lines.note: The expression is used in letters to convey thanks. The alternative 'or ...' leads to the statement about expressing pleasure below.

runs.text: moſtra alegrarſe com algũa couſa em reſpeito

lines.note: The writer may instead show pleasure about something involving another person. The social relationship that limits this usage is given on the following row.
The expression concerns people of lower status. Inferior corrects OCR infertor; this is the historical usage restriction reported by the dictionary.
Hai and mi connect ash with the body. The gloss begins the body's ending or dissolution, continued below; the printed Fai mi spacing is retained without adding a comma.

runs.text: o corpo em poo, ou cinza.

lines.note: The body is reduced to dust or ashes. This completes the first Quaijin entry and distinguishes it from the following ash-and-embers sense.

Hai and moekui explain ash and a burnt or burning remnant of wood. Focused enlargement supports Portuguese tição, including the cedilla and the tilde over a; the following example confirms the ash-and-charcoal context.
Dooja mina quaijin to natta says that all the temples and shrines became ashes. The scan supplies the paragraph mark omitted by OCR and shows Todos without a secure nasal mark.

runs.text: os tẽplos, & ermidas dos Camis ſe queimarão,

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies temples and shrines of the kami that burned. Camis is the Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is flagged for optional whole-word typeface review.
The buildings were turned into ash and charcoal. This finishes the past-event example; the Portuguese historical endings are not reinterpreted as modern future-tense instructions.
Quaijit denotes the last day of the month. Its final t is retained as a checked coda, not expanded to a modern syllable.
Quaiju is simply identified as a tree so called. The scan supports the double-s sort in aßi rather than OCR aſi; the gloss itself does not establish a species.
Ai chigiru means pledging or entering a mutual bond. The gloss gives friendship or peace; pa- begins pazes below.

runs.text: zes que ſe fazem entre algũs.

lines.note: The peace or alliance is made among a number of people. The nasal abbreviation in algũs is retained without expansion.
Quaimon is identified only as a particular dignity or office. The brief gloss does not establish which rank, so the note does not supply one.
Hi no oshite identifies a mark impressed with fire. The Portuguese describes a brand, with the manner and location continued below.
The brand is put on the body, face, and so forth. Quain wo begins the verbal example; the aligned roſto allograph is retained rather than mechanically changing the st types throughout the page.
The alternatives atsuru and osu describe applying or stamping the brand. Portuguese a- begins animaes, making clear that the example also concerns branding animals.
Nimaes completes animaes. This is a continuation of the branding example, not a separate zoological headword.
Quaina describes something grand, showy, or liberal. The damaged initial has the tail of Q and belongs to the single headword, not OCR o uaina.
Liberalidade completes the alternative sense of generosity or liberality. It leads naturally into the following descriptions of a generous, ostentatious person.
Quaina hito is followed by the preferred alternative Quaxita hito. Potiùs is italic Latin apparatus meaning 'rather'; Ho- starts the Portuguese person-description below.

runs.text: mem que folga de fazer oſtentação, & apa-

lines.note: The person delights in display and outward magnificence. Apa- begins aparato at the next line, preserving the physical break.
Rato completes aparato, while ſendo liberal explains generosity in giving. The scan supports ſendo rather than OCR ſeudo. Ki no quai- begins a second Japanese example.
Na completes ki no quaina hito, again paired with quaxita hito. The Portuguese calls this a generous person and continues the characterization below.
Grandioſo completes the generous-and-magnificent description. Its sense belongs to the preceding person's disposition, not to the pregnancy entry that follows.
Quainin means pregnancy. Quainin shita begins the example of a pregnant woman, with the noun nhonin on the following row.
Nhonin completes the Japanese phrase for the pregnant woman. The following Quai- begins another pregnancy expression; q̃ remains the printed Portuguese abbreviation.

The completed expression is Quainin de gozaru, 'be pregnant'. The native row has nin de, not OCR ninade; removing the spurious a restores the visible text without altering the phrase's historical form.
Quaiqi is recovery of health, explained through a sound or agreeable condition. The Portuguese continues with the former state of health below.
The definition is regaining one's previous health. Quaiqi wo uru and the following quaiqi suru are alternative expressions; the damaged Q remains part of a single word.
Suru completes the second recovery expression. It is a real short Japanese continuation, not an independent verb headword here.
Quaiqiǔ denotes remembering past things. The following row specifies deceased people, narrowing the memorial context of this entry.
Quaiqiǔ no renga is linked verse composed in remembrance of the dead. Ver- begins verſos; the Japanese renga here is part of a standalone example, not an embedded Portuguese term.

runs.text: ſos que hum faz por lembrança, & memoria

lines.note: The verses are made for remembrance and memory. The scan does not show the baseline's period after memoria, and the phrase continues directly with the people commemorated below.
Dalguns defunctos identifies the deceased being remembered. The close historical spelling is retained rather than expanded to de alguns.
Meguri kitaru means coming round or coming by a circuitous route. The Portuguese gives the same circling movement.
Às voltas supplies the alternative 'in turns or circuits'. The grave is retained, and the row completes Quairai rather than the puppeteer entry below.
Quairaixi is a performer who makes puppets dance. Bonifrates is the Portuguese puppet term; no additional kind of puppet mechanism is inferred.
Quairin means a reply to a letter. Repoſta is the printed historical spelling, not silently expanded to resposta; S. is an upright register label.
Meguru hisashi describes a surrounding or connecting eaved passage. The Portuguese identifies a passageway and continues its purpose below.

runs.text: pera paßar de hũa caſa a outra.

lines.note: The passage allows movement from one building to another. The marked hũa and historical pera are kept as printed.
Quairocu means losing one's wealth through its burning. The scan supports continuous Quairocu and riquezas rather than OCR Q uairocu and rique zas.
Quairocu no nan ni vǒ describes encountering the disaster of a fire loss. The abbreviated cõ begins the corresponding Portuguese phrase about meeting with misfortune.

runs.text: trabalhos, & perdas de fazenda q̃ ſe queimou.

lines.note: The misfortune consists of troubles and loss of property that burned. Fazenda here is possessions or wealth, not necessarily a farm.
Tsugomori and tsuitachi identify the last and first days of a month. Derra- begins derradeiro across the line break.
This completes the last-and-first-day pairing. The order agrees with the two Japanese explanations rather than reversing them to ordinary calendar order.
Quaitai is equated with Quainin, pregnancy. The comma after i is visible; the Portuguese subject is completed by molher on the next row.
Molher completes 'the woman being pregnant'. This row belongs to the pregnancy synonym and not to the following ship entry.
Quaixen is a merchant vessel. The initial Q belongs to the headword, and mer- begins the Portuguese merchants word below.
Cadores completes mercadores, specifying the vessel's commercial association. The source gives no vessel size or rig to add.
Quaixeqi is defined as a house or place for gatherings and recreation. Fol- begins folguedo on the following physical row.
Guedo completes the recreation gloss. Quaixeqi wo suru is introduced, then Me- starts the editorial Meliùs indicating a preferred expression.
Meliùs recommends Quai wo suru rather than the preceding expression. The printed close eſteajuntamen- is retained; the Portuguese gathering word continues below.

runs.text: to, ou pera beber Cha, ou pera fazer verſos.

lines.note: The gathering may be for drinking tea or composing verses. Cha is retained in the italic Portuguese wording; this line does not introduce a standalone Japanese example.

runs.text: Papel em que ſe eſcreuem certos ver-

lines.note: Quaixi is paper on which certain verses are written. Ver- begins verſos, and the next row identifies the type of poetry.

runs.text: ſos que chamão rengas em hũs ajuntamentos que

lines.note: The verses are called rengas and are written at particular gatherings. Rengas is the Japanese genre-name embedded, with Portuguese plural marking, in the Portuguese explanation; it is flagged for whole-word typeface review.
Fazem completes the relative clause about holding those gatherings. The short row finishes Quaixi before the following meeting-house entry.
Quaixo is a designated house or room for consultation. The lower-right Quai- is a separate catchword, not a continuation of this completed definition.
